previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease and a history of multiple transplants was admitted for removal of her peritoneal dialysis catheter due to inadequate volume clearance as a rapid transporter. She had transitioned to hemodialysis and elected to have the catheter removed. The procedure was performed on 2193-08-06 without complications. Postoperatively, she was started on a heparin drip for anticoagulation bridging due to her mechanical mitral valve. Warfarin was resumed the following day, and her INR rose from 2.1 to 3.0 by discharge. She tolerated diet, had a bowel movement with assistance, and completed a hemodialysis session with 2 liters of fluid removed. She remained stable, alert, and ambulatory throughout her stay. She was discharged home on her prior medications, including warfarin 6 mg daily, with instructions to follow up with the coagulation clinic and resume outpatient hemodialysis.

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to Dr. ___ 
___ for evaluation and treatment of a left foot infection. 
The patient underwent a diagnostic angiogram on ___, which 
went well without complications (reader referred to the 
Operative Note for details). After a brief, uneventful stay in 
the PACU, the patient arrived on the floor NPO, and on IV 
fluids.  The patient was hemodynamically stable.

Neuro: When tolerating oral intake, the patient was transitioned 
to oral pain medications. CV: The patient remained stable from a 
cardiovascular standpoint; vital signs were routinely monitored. 
Pulmonary: The patient remained stable from a pulmonary 
standpoint; vital signs were routinely monitored. Good pulmonary 
toilet, early ambulation and incentive spirrometry were 
encouraged throughout hospitalization. GI/GU/FEN: Diet was 
advanced when appropriate, which was well tolerated.  Patient's 
intake and output were closely monitored, and IV fluid was 
adjusted when necessary.  Electrolytes were routinely followed, 
and repleted when necessary. ID: The patient's white blood count 
and fever curves were closely watched for signs of infection.  
The patient's groin dressing was removed and will remain off to 
room air. The patient was continued on IV abx throughout the 
hospital stay and will continue on IV Vancomycin on dialysis 
days until follow up with Dr. ___. Wound: The Podiatry 
___ was consulted for evaluation of her wound. The team 
defferred surgical intervention to patient's primary DPM. Per 
the patient request, a felted foam dressing was applied to the 
patient's L foot prior to discharge. Hematology: The patient's 
complete blood count was examined routinely; no transfusions 
were required. Prophylaxis: The patient received a heparin gtt, 
coumadin, and venodyne boots were used during this stay; was 
encouraged to get up and ambulate as early as possible. The 
heparin dtt was d/c'd once the patient had a therapeutic INR. 
The patient was discharged with an INR 3.1. Nutrition: The 
patient requested a nutrition consult on ___. Nutrition saw 
the patient and the patient refused. 

At the time of discharge, the patient was doing well, afebrile 
with stable vital signs.  The patient was tolerating a regular 
diet, ambulating, voiding without assistance, and pain was well 
controlled.  The patient received discharge teaching and 
follow-up instructions with understanding verbalized and 
agreement with the discharge plan. The patient will follow up 
with Dr. ___ a scheduled left femoral endarterectomy on 
___. The patient will be admitted 2 days prior to start a 
heparin gtt to ensure anticoagulation while off coumadin.

Discharge Instructions:
Ms. ___,

The patient was admitted to Dr. ___

MEDICATION:
Take Aspirin 325mg (enteric coated) once daily 
Continue all other medications you were taking before surgery, 
unless otherwise directed
You make take Tylenol or prescribed pain medications for any 
post procedure pain or discomfort
You are given a prescription for IV Vancomycin to be 
administered when you go to dialysis. 
You are given a prescription for nausea. Please take as 
directed. 
WHAT TO EXPECT:
It is normal to have slight swelling of the legs:
Elevate your leg above the level of your heart with pillows 
every ___ hours throughout the day and night
Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your 
legs elevated
It is normal to feel tired and have a decreased appetite, your 
appetite will return with time 
Drink plenty of fluids and eat small frequent meals
It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber, 
lean meats, vegetables/fruits, low fat, low cholesterol) to 
maintain your strength and assist in wound healing
To avoid constipation: eat a high fiber diet and use stool 
softener while taking pain medication

ACTIVITIES:
When you go home, you may walk and use stairs
You may shower (let the soapy water run over groin incision, 
rinse and pat dry)
Your incision may be left uncovered, unless you have small 
amounts of drainage from the wound, then place a dry dressing or 

band aid over the area 
No heavy lifting, pushing or pulling (greater than 5 lbs) for 
1 week (to allow groin puncture to heal)
After 1 week, you may resume sexual activity
After 1 week, gradually increase your activities and distance 
walked as you can tolerate
No driving until you are no longer taking pain medications
You are able to walk with the L foot protective offloading 
pad. Please keep the pad on until you are able to follow up with 
your outside hospital podiatrist. You can change the outer 
dressing as needed. 

CALL THE OFFICE FOR: ___
Numbness, coldness or pain in lower extremities 
Temperature greater than 101.5F for 24 hours
New or increased drainage from incision or white, yellow or 
green drainage from incisions
Bleeding from groin puncture site

pressure to area for 10 minutes. If bleeding stops, call 
vascular office ___. If bleeding does not stop, call

RIGHT FOOT:  There has been resection of the second toe at the MTP joint,

On the lateral view, there is a rockerbottom-type deformity of the mid foot.

LEFT FOOT:  There are no signs for acute fractures or dislocations.  There are
vascular calcifications.  There is a healed fracture deformity of the fifth
metatarsal base.  Small erosion is seen at the head of the fifth proximal
phalanx.  There is soft tissue swelling overlying the forefoot at the level of
the metatarsal heads.  No soft tissue gas or definite bone destruction is seen
to be suggestive of radiographic signs for acute osteomyelitis.  If there is
high concern, MRI could be performed.
